title: Confidence Interval Laboratory
summary: A simulated population with a true mean of exactly 12. Each study draws its own sample and reports its own interval, the intervals stack up against the fixed truth, and only one of the three controls changes how often they contain it.
learningObjectives: Describe coverage as a property of the procedure across many studies rather than of one interval.
Predict what sample size and population spread do to interval width.
Explain why neither changes coverage, and why the confidence level does.
Explain why a single interval either contains the true value or does not, and why you cannot tell which.
State why the common probability sentence about a confidence interval is the wrong one.
interactionTypes: repeated simulated studies against a fixed true value
stacked interval plot with misses drawn dashed
running coverage reported against the level asked for
confidence level, sample size and population spread as separate controls
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Intervals that miss the true value are drawn dashed rather than merely recoloured, so the distinction survives greyscale. The figure marks the true value with a labelled line and its description states the level, how many studies were run, how many contain the truth and the resulting coverage. All three headline figures are text. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated. The population has a true mean change of exactly 12 minutes of walking per day by construction, which is knowable only because the activity invented it. No real trial, participant or dataset is represented.
simulationNotes: Each study draws n observations from Normal(12, sigma) and reports the sample mean plus or minus z times sigma over the square root of n, with z the normal quantile for the chosen level. Sigma is treated as known because the simulation states it, which is why the multiplier is a normal quantile and why every interval in a run has exactly the same width: the only thing that varies from study to study is where the interval sits. Nominal coverage is exact under this model, so about the level percentage of intervals contain the true mean whatever n and sigma are. A real study estimates sigma from its own sample and uses a t multiplier, which widens intervals at small samples and makes their widths vary. Coverage is exact here only because the model is exactly right; real coverage degrades when the assumptions do.
readmeTopic: what the ninety-five per cent in a confidence interval refers to
